In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''scheme-theoretic intersection''' of closed subschemes ''X'', ''Y'' of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''W'' is <math>X \times_W Y</math>, the [[fiber product]] of the [[closed immersion]]s <math>X \hookrightarrow W, Y \hookrightarrow W</math>. It is denoted by <math>X \cap Y</math>.

Locally, ''W'' is given as <math>\operatorname{Spec} R</math> for some ring ''R'' and ''X'', ''Y'' as <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R/I), \operatorname{Spec}(R/J)</math> for some ideals ''I'', ''J''. Thus, locally, the intersection <math>X \cap Y</math> is given as
:<math>\operatorname{Spec}(R/(I+J)).</math>
Here, we used <math>R/I \otimes_R R/J \simeq R/(I + J)</math> (for this identity, see [[tensor product of modules#Examples]].)

'''Example''': Let <math>X \subset \mathbb{P}^n</math> be a [[projective variety]] with the homogeneous coordinate ring ''S/I'', where ''S'' is a polynomial ring. If <math>H = \{ f = 0 \} \subset \mathbb{P}^n</math> is a [[hypersurface]] defined by some homogeneous polynomial ''f'' in ''S'', then

: <math>X \cap H = \operatorname{Proj}(S/(I, f)).</math>

If ''f'' is linear (deg = 1), it is called a [[hyperplane section]]. See also: [[Bertini's theorem]].<!-- this is not the best place to discuss the theorem. -->

Now, a scheme-theoretic intersection may not be a ''correct'' intersection, say, from the point of view of [[intersection theory]]. For example,<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Appendix A: Example 1.1.1.}}</ref> let <math>W = \operatorname{Spec}(k[x, y, z, w])</math> be the affine 4-space and ''X'', ''Y'' closed subschemes defined by the ideals <math>(x, y) \cap (z, w)</math> and <math>(x - z, y - w)</math>. Since ''X'' is the union of two planes, each intersecting with ''Y'' at the origin with multiplicity one, by the linearity of [[intersection multiplicity]], we expect ''X'' and ''Y'' intersect at the origin with multiplicity two. On the other hand, one sees the scheme-theoretic intersection <math>X \cap Y</math> consists of the origin with multiplicity three. That is, a scheme-theoretic multiplicity of an intersection may differ from an intersection-theoretic multiplicity, the latter given by [[Intersection number#Serre's Tor formula|Serre's Tor formula]]. Solving this disparity is one of the starting points for [[derived algebraic geometry]], which aims to introduce the notion of [[derived intersection]].

== Proper intersection ==
Let ''X'' be a [[regular scheme]] and ''V'', ''W'' closed integral subschemes. Then an irreducible component ''P'' of <math>V \cap W := V \times_X W</math> is called '''proper''' if the [[Serre's inequality on height|inequality (due to Serre)]]:
:<math>\operatorname{codim}(P, X) \le \operatorname{codim}(V, X) + \operatorname{codim}(W, X)</math>
is an equality.<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=§ 20.4.}}</ref> The intersection <math>V \cap W</math> is proper if every irreducible component of it is proper (in particular, the empty intersection is considered proper.) Two [[algebraic cycle]]s are said to intersect properly if the varieties in the cycles intersect properly.

For example, two [[Divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisors]] (codimension-one cycles) on a smooth variety intersect properly if and only if they share no common irreducible component. [[Chow's moving lemma]] (on a smooth variety) says that an intersection can be made proper after replacing a divisor by a suitable linearly equivalent divisor (cf. [[Kleiman's theorem]].)

Serre's inequality above may fail in general for a non-regular ambient scheme. For example,<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 7.1.6.}}</ref> let <math>X = \operatorname{Spec} k[x, y, z, w]/(xz - yw), \, V = V(\overline{x}, \overline{y}), \, W = V(\overline{z}, \overline{w})</math>. Then <math>V, W</math> have codimension one, while <math>V \cap W</math> has codimension three.

Some authors such as Bloch define a proper intersection without assuming ''X'' is regular: in the notations as above, a component ''P'' is proper if
:<math>\operatorname{codim}(P, X) \ge \operatorname{codim}(V, X) + \operatorname{codim}(W, X).</math>
